newsitem.title: USA: Senate Majority Leader sets out Republican agenda.
newsitem.headline: Senate Majority Leader sets out Republican agenda.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott outlined the Republican agenda Sunday, saying a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution would be the first Senate bill introduced when lawmakers return later this month.

Senate Republicans met for 12 hours at the end of last week to carve out the agenda, which will also put a high priority on the issues of education, crime and drugs, Lott said on CBS Television's "Face the Nation."

The balanced budget amendment appears to have the votes for passage in the Senate, Lott, R-Miss., said. The measure passed the House of Representatives last year, but failed by one vote in the Senate.
Senate Republicans are expected to vote for the amendment to require the federal budget be balanced and they plan to meet with Democratic colleagues who also want to see the measure passed, he said.
Lott said he has had some "good conversations" with President Clinton about reaching a balanced budget in 2002, but he called a reported Clinton proposal on Medicare "troublesome."

The Washington Post Sunday reported the White House is considering substantial cuts in premiums Medicare pays to HMOs as part of a plan to keep the federal health insurance programme for the elderly afloat.
The newspaper said the proposal was one part of the administration's overall plan to cut growth of Medicare by about $100 billion over the next five years.
Lott said he had not seen any details of the reported proposal but added that it looked like a "shell game."
Clinton is scheduled to release his budget in February.
"We're very worried that he's going to allow spending to actually go up before it supposedly comes down and the deficit to go up before it actually comes down," Lott said.

"This is going to be an important test for the president and it's going to be very symbolically important to us about how he wants to work with us and deal with us to accomplish what needs to be accomplished with the budget," he added.
If Clinton comes out with "a real tough budget ... we're going to get off to a good start," Lott said.
On health care, Republicans will continue to work on "affordability and access," Lott said.
A "family friendly workplace" to give people an opportunity to have flexible schedules so they can spend time with their children would also be a key agenda item, Lott said.

Campaign finance reform will be worked on "early, quickly," and the Rules Committee will hold hearings on the issue, he said. A Republican task force was set up Friday to decide what areas Republicans agree on for improving campaigns in the future, Lott said.
Republicans are likely to want bigger tax cuts than what Clinton has indicated in the past, he said.
Tax cuts over the next five years of $100 billion would be too low, while $200 billion would be "closer to where I'd like to see it," Lott said.
Tax credit for families with children, estate tax relief, and a capital gains tax rate cut, were areas he singled out.
